title: Bebe Nanaki and Jai Ram
hookLine: his sister and her husband took Nanak to Sultanpur and found him work

lines: THINGS AREN'T GOING WELL AT HOME.
cards: Back home, things aren't going well. The young man gives away what he's meant to sell. He sits for hours with wandering holy men.
His father is running out of patience. Then a message comes from another town. His older sister has married and moved away, and she and her husband have a room, and maybe a job.
Come stay with us, she says.

teach.h: BEBE: AN ELDER SISTER, WITH LOVE.
teach.b: Bebe Nanaki was Guru Nanak's older sister. Bebe is an affectionate word for an elder sister, and Sikhs still say her name with it.
In the janamsakhis, she's the one in the family who seems to see her brother clearly from the start: where others saw a boy who wouldn't settle, the stories have her seeing something holy.
She married Jai Ram, who, tradition says, worked in Sultanpur for the local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi. And here help becomes practical.
Jai Ram used his place to find his wife's brother a job in the modikhana, the government storehouse where grain was kept and given out. Not a glamorous detail: a brother-in-law making a call.
The stories say Nanak did the work honestly and well. And they tell one well-known moment from that storehouse.
Weighing out grain, counting each measure aloud, he came to the number tera, which in Punjabi also means yours.
Tradition says he stopped counting and kept saying it: tera, tera, yours, yours, everything is Yours.

teach.h: A SPARE ROOM AND AN INTRODUCTION.
teach.b: It was in Sultanpur, too, in the stories, that his great turning came. But notice who got him there. Not a king or a priest.
A sister who believed in him, and a brother-in-law who opened a door.
Family who helps doesn't always look like a sermon. Sometimes it's a spare room and an introduction.

how: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki in the stories of Guru Nanak's life, and the tera, tera story from the Sultanpur storehouse is told to children as a lesson that everything belongs to God.

o: an aunt who raised Guru Nanak

s: Jai Ram found Nanak work in the governor's storehouse
tradition says Jai Ram worked for Daulat Khan Lodi and found him work in the modikhana.
in the stories, Nanaki was the last in the family to see who her brother was
she's the one who seems to see him clearly from the start.
tera means both a number and yours in Punjabi
tradition says Nanak kept repeating it: tera, tera, everything is Yours.

games.q: you're Nanaki. your younger brother isn't settling at home and your father is losing patience. what do you do?
o: tell him to grow up and listen to your father.
stay out of it; it's your parents' business.
invite him to stay with you, and have your husband help find him work.
games.why: in the stories, Nanaki and Jai Ram bring him to Sultanpur and find him work in the storehouse, where his great turning comes.

practice: Bring to mind a brother or sister, or a cousin or friend who's close as one, and where they might be stuck right now: not what's wrong with them, but what door might be closed in front of them.
Ask what small door you could open: a message, a name, a ride, a room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you breathe out.

wordCard.voice: Bebe Nanaki. Guru Nanak's older sister, who, with her husband Jai Ram, welcomed him to Sultanpur and found him work in the storehouse.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tera, yours; in the storehouse story, also the number he was counting.

carryVoice: Your line: family who helps. Tera, tera: yours, yours, all of it. Day eight hundred three, done.
